# Methods: how Public Journal Club reviews a paper

<!-- Generated by scripts/build-methods-doc.mjs from config/rubric.json (rubric version 1). Edit those files, not this one, then run `npm run docs`. -->

Rubric version: **1**. Every saved review records the rubric version it was rated with (`rubric_version` in its `review.json`).

This document is for scientists who want to check how reviews are produced. Reviews are written by large language models (Claude). They are a teaching aid that models how scientists weigh evidence, not a substitute for expert appraisal. The rubric below constrains the models, and several steps are checked by deterministic code rather than left to the model.

## Pipeline

1. **Text extraction.** The PDF's text is extracted (`unpdf`) so quotes can be verified later, and the paper's DOI is read from its first two pages.
2. **Publication status (deterministic).** The DOI is looked up in the Crossref REST API, which includes the Retraction Watch database. Retractions, withdrawals, expressions of concern and corrections are read from the paper's `updated-by` relations and from notices whose `update-to` points at the paper. Crossref records of type `posted-content` are reported as preprints. See [Crossref and Retraction Watch](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/retrieve-metadata/retraction-watch/).
3. **Background check (Sonnet, 2 web searches).** Paper details, the authors' financial or professional stakes in the result, the journal's standing, and earlier work or replication attempts.
4. **Critique (Opus, no web search, with a code sandbox)** and, at the same time, **context (Sonnet, 2 web searches)**. The critique classifies the paper, writes the highlights, and scores the four ratings using the rubric below. The context step writes the plain-language summary and compares the findings with related research.
5. **Server-side checks.** The cap on "evidence for the main claim" is applied in code (the model's score is lowered if it exceeds the cap, and the original score is kept as `capped_from`). Every quoted passage is matched against the PDF text; unmatched quotes get one repair attempt and are otherwise flagged as unverified and not highlighted. Claims that a number was recomputed with code are kept only if the model actually ran code during the critique.
6. **Glossary (Sonnet).** Plain definitions for terms used in the finished review.

## Step 1: classify the paper

The critique first records the paper's **evidence type** (its design), its **main claim** in one sentence, the **type of claim**, and the **population** studied. It also flags **overreach**: a main claim that goes beyond what the design can support.

| Claim type | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Cause or treatment effect (`causal`) | Says X causes, prevents or treats Y in people (for example 'yoga poses reverse scoliosis'). |
| Link or association (`associational`) | Says X is linked to Y, without claiming one causes the other (for example 'a variant is associated with higher risk'). |
| How something works (`mechanistic`) | Explains a biological mechanism, usually in cells, animals or another model system. |
| Test or prediction (`diagnostic`) | Says a test, score or model can detect or predict an outcome. |
| Description (`descriptive`) | Reports how common something is, or what was observed, without explaining why. |

## Step 2: caps by design and claim

"Evidence for the main claim" can never exceed the cap for the paper's evidence type and claim type. The cap expresses what the best possible study of that design could show for that kind of claim. The score then starts from the cap and is lowered for flaws, imprecision, or conflict with other research, in the spirit of [GRADE](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.39489.470347.AD) and the [OCEBM Levels of Evidence](https://www.cebm.ox.ac.uk/resources/levels-of-evidence/ocebm-levels-of-evidence).

| Evidence type | Cause or treatment effect | Link or association | How something works | Test or prediction | Description | Appraisal tools |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Meta-analysis of randomized trials | 5 | 5 | 4 | 4.5 | 5 | [AMSTAR 2](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.j4008), [GRADE](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.39489.470347.AD) |
| Randomized trial | 4.5 | 4.5 | 3.5 | 4 | 4.5 | [RoB 2](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l4898) |
| Observational study with a causal design | 3.5 | 4 | 3 | 3.5 | 4 | [ROBINS-I](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i4919), [STROBE-MR](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2021.18236), [Target trial emulation](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwv254) |
| Observational study | 3 | 4 | 2.5 | 3.5 | 4.5 | [ROBINS-E](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2024.108602), [Newcastle-Ottawa Scale](https://www.ohri.ca/programs/clinical_epidemiology/oxford.asp) |
| Genetic association study | 2 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 4 | [STREGA](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000022), [Replicating associations](https://doi.org/10.1038/447655a), [Genome-wide significance](https://doi.org/10.1002/gepi.20303), [Ancestry representation](https://doi.org/10.1038/538161a) |
| Diagnostic or prediction model study | 2.5 | 4 | 2 | 4 | 4 | [QUADAS-2](https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-155-8-201110180-00009), [PROBAST](https://doi.org/10.7326/M18-1376) |
| Laboratory or animal study | 2 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 4 | [SYRCLE risk of bias](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-14-43), [ARRIVE 2.0](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000410) |
| Case report or case series | 1.5 | 1.5 | 1.5 | 1.5 | 2.5 | [CARE](https://doi.org/10.1186/1752-1947-7-223), [JBI case series checklist](https://doi.org/10.11124/JBISRIR-D-19-00099) |
| Narrative review or commentary | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | [OCEBM Levels of Evidence](https://www.cebm.ox.ac.uk/resources/levels-of-evidence/ocebm-levels-of-evidence) |
| Other design | 3 | 3.5 | 3.5 | 3.5 | 4 | [OCEBM Levels of Evidence](https://www.cebm.ox.ac.uk/resources/levels-of-evidence/ocebm-levels-of-evidence) |

- **Randomized trial:** A single trial is capped below 5 because one trial, however good, still needs replication.
- **Observational study:** Causal claims are capped at 3 because people choose their own exposures, so other differences between groups can explain the result.
- **Genetic association study:** Association claims can be strong with replication. Causal or clinical claims are capped at 2 because an associated variant is not necessarily the causal one, and associations don't establish clinical usefulness.
- **Diagnostic or prediction model study:** Diagnostic claims are capped at 4; reserve 4 for models validated independently in a different setting.
- **Laboratory or animal study:** Mechanistic claims about the model system can score up to 4. Claims about human treatment are capped at 2 because most findings in animals and cells don't carry over to people.
- **Case report or case series:** Without a comparison group, a case series can't show that a treatment caused an outcome.
- **Narrative review or commentary:** A review that isn't systematic can't be stronger than the evidence it chooses to cite.

## Step 3: checklists by design

Study quality is judged against the best version of the paper's own design, using a short checklist drawn from the established appraisal tool for that design. The checklists are deliberately brief, plain-language paraphrases; they are not substitutes for the full tools.

### Meta-analysis of randomized trials

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses that pool randomized trials. Based on [AMSTAR 2](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.j4008), [GRADE](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.39489.470347.AD).

- Was the question and protocol registered in advance?
- Was the literature search thorough, and were unpublished studies sought?
- Did the authors assess risk of bias in each included trial, and account for it?
- Were the pooled studies similar enough to combine (heterogeneity)?
- Was publication bias assessed?

### Randomized trial

Participants assigned to groups by chance. Based on [RoB 2](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l4898).

- Was assignment truly random and concealed until enrollment?
- Were participants, carers and outcome assessors blinded where possible?
- How many dropped out, and were all randomized participants analysed?
- Was the primary outcome pre-registered and reported as planned?
- Is the sample large enough for the effect claimed?

### Observational study with a causal design

Mendelian randomization, natural experiments, target trial emulation. Based on [ROBINS-I](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i4919), [STROBE-MR](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2021.18236), [Target trial emulation](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwv254).

- Are the design's key assumptions stated and tested (for example instrument validity in Mendelian randomization)?
- Is the comparison clearly defined, with a clear start of follow-up?
- Were sensitivity analyses run for the main assumptions?
- Could the result be explained by selection into the study or loss to follow-up?

### Observational study

Cohort, case-control, cross-sectional and biobank or health-record studies. Based on [ROBINS-E](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2024.108602), [Newcastle-Ottawa Scale](https://www.ohri.ca/programs/clinical_epidemiology/oxford.asp).

- Were the groups comparable at the start, and how were they selected?
- Were important other explanations (confounders) measured and adjusted for?
- Were exposure and outcome measured the same way in every group?
- How complete was follow-up?
- Do the authors use causal language the design can't support?

### Genetic association study

GWAS, exome-wide association, rare-variant burden tests, family-based association. Based on [STREGA](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000022), [Replicating associations](https://doi.org/10.1038/447655a), [Genome-wide significance](https://doi.org/10.1002/gepi.20303), [Ancestry representation](https://doi.org/10.1038/538161a).

- Was the significance threshold corrected for the number of tests (for example genome-wide significance)?
- Was the finding replicated in an independent sample?
- Was population structure or relatedness controlled?
- Which ancestries were studied, and does the claim generalize beyond them?
- For rare variants: how were variants called, filtered and classified?

### Diagnostic or prediction model study

Test accuracy studies, risk scores, clinical prediction and machine-learning models. Based on [QUADAS-2](https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-155-8-201110180-00009), [PROBAST](https://doi.org/10.7326/M18-1376).

- Were participants representative of the people the test is meant for?
- Was the reference standard applied to everyone, blind to the test result?
- Was the model validated on data it was not built from, ideally from another setting?
- Are accuracy, calibration and the number of events reported?

### Laboratory or animal study

Cell culture, organoids, animal models. Based on [SYRCLE risk of bias](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-14-43), [ARRIVE 2.0](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000410).

- Were animals or samples randomized to groups, and were assessors blinded?
- Was the sample size justified, and were experiments independently repeated?
- Were appropriate controls used?
- Are all outcomes and excluded animals or samples reported?
- How far is the model from the human condition the paper talks about?

### Case report or case series

Descriptions of one patient or a group of patients without a comparison group. Based on [CARE](https://doi.org/10.1186/1752-1947-7-223), [JBI case series checklist](https://doi.org/10.11124/JBISRIR-D-19-00099).

- Were cases included consecutively, with clear criteria?
- Is the condition and its measurement described in enough detail?
- Is follow-up complete and long enough?
- Are alternative explanations for the outcome discussed?

### Narrative review or commentary

Reviews without a systematic search, opinion pieces, perspectives. Based on [OCEBM Levels of Evidence](https://www.cebm.ox.ac.uk/resources/levels-of-evidence/ocebm-levels-of-evidence).

- Are the claims supported by cited primary studies?
- Does the review present evidence on both sides?
- Does it distinguish strong evidence from weak?

### Other design

Qualitative research, methods papers, simulations, or designs that don't fit above. Based on [OCEBM Levels of Evidence](https://www.cebm.ox.ac.uk/resources/levels-of-evidence/ocebm-levels-of-evidence).

- Is the method appropriate for the question?
- Is it compared against existing approaches or a reasonable baseline?
- Could someone else reproduce it from what is reported?

## Step 4: the four ratings

Each rating is scored from 0 to 5 in steps of 0.5 against fixed anchors.

### Study quality (`rigor`, higher is better)

How well the study was carried out, judged against the best possible version of its own design (use the checklist for its evidence type). A well-run observational study can score high here even though its causal claims are capped. See [RoB 2](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l4898), [ROBINS-I](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i4919), [ROBINS-E](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2024.108602), [AMSTAR 2](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.j4008), [QUADAS-2](https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-155-8-201110180-00009), [PROBAST](https://doi.org/10.7326/M18-1376), [SYRCLE risk of bias](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-14-43).

| Score | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 5 | No meaningful flaws for this design. |
| 4 | Minor flaws, unlikely to change the conclusion. |
| 3 | Flaws that could change the size of the effect, but probably not its direction. |
| 2 | Serious flaws that could explain the result on their own. |
| 1 | Flaws so severe the result can't be interpreted. |
| 0 | Not a real test of the question. |

### Risk of slanted reporting (`bias`, higher is worse)

Risks that study quality doesn't cover: conflicts of interest and funding, selective reporting of outcomes or analyses, and spin (conclusions, abstract or title that go beyond the results). See [Spin](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1710755115), [Industry sponsorship](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.MR000033.pub3).

| Score | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 5 | Reporting is so slanted that the paper can't be taken at face value. |
| 4 | Several of the above, and they push in the direction the authors favour. |
| 3 | Clear spin, or outcomes that seem selectively reported, or an undeclared relevant conflict. |
| 2 | Some spin or a relevant conflict, but the main results are reported fairly. |
| 1 | Minor issues, such as a declared conflict with no sign it shaped the reporting. |
| 0 | Independent authors, outcomes reported as planned, conclusions match the results. |

### Evidence for the main claim (`effect`, higher is better)

How strongly the paper supports its own main claim. First identify the main claim and its type. The score can't exceed the cap for this evidence type and claim type, and is lowered further for flaws, imprecision, or results that conflict with other research. See [GRADE](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.39489.470347.AD), [OCEBM Levels of Evidence](https://www.cebm.ox.ac.uk/resources/levels-of-evidence/ocebm-levels-of-evidence).

| Score | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 5 | Strong, consistent evidence that would be hard to overturn. |
| 4 | Good evidence; further research is unlikely to reverse it. |
| 3 | Moderate evidence; the claim is plausible but could change. |
| 2 | Weak evidence; consistent with the claim but other explanations remain likely. |
| 1 | Very weak evidence; the data barely bear on the claim. |
| 0 | No evidence for the claim, or the data point the other way. |

### Usefulness (`value`, higher is better)

What the paper is good for: changing practice, informing decisions alongside other evidence, or pointing to what should be tested next.

| Score | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 5 | Practice-changing; requires strong, replicated evidence in the people it applies to. |
| 4 | Should inform decisions alongside other evidence. |
| 3 | Adds meaningfully to the evidence on its question. |
| 2 | Worth testing further; a reason to run a better study. |
| 1 | Adds little that wasn't known. |
| 0 | No usable contribution. |

Study quality and the risk of slanted reporting are scored separately on purpose: the first covers how the study was run, the second covers conflicts of interest, selective reporting and spin, which a well-run study can still have. Each review must also include at least 2 genuine strengths.

## Recomputing reported numbers

Statistical reporting errors are common and can be detected by recomputing reported values from the paper's own numbers ([Recomputing reported statistics](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-015-0664-2); [GRIM test](https://doi.org/10.1177/1948550616673876)). Before a review says a reported number is wrong, the critique model must recompute it, using a code sandbox for anything beyond simple arithmetic. Each such note shows what the paper reported, the inputs, the method and the result, and whether code was used. If code was not actually run during the critique, the note is shown as checked by hand.

## Limitations

- Ratings are model judgments guided by the rubric. They have not yet been validated against independent expert raters; a planned calibration set (a randomized trial, a meta-analysis, an observational study, an animal study and a genetic association study) is the next step.
- The caps are the authors' judgment, informed by the cited frameworks, and are open to revision.
- Background checks rely on what web search finds; undisclosed conflicts of interest can be missed.
- Publication status depends on Crossref and Retraction Watch coverage and on the DOI being present in the PDF.

## Changing the rubric

Everything above comes from `config/rubric.json`: claim types, evidence types, checklists, caps, rating definitions, anchors and citations. To change it, edit that file, bump its `version`, and run `npm run docs` to regenerate this document. The app validates the file at startup and refuses to run if, for example, an evidence type is missing a cap or cites an unknown reference. Bumping the version means each paper gets a fresh review the next time it is uploaded.
